documents.summary: A compaction or handoff drops still-needed task state from the receiving agent's input, causing it to repeat discovery, lose constraints, or ask again for existing authorization.
documents.title: Context handoff loss

content.name: summary
content: A compaction or handoff drops still-needed task state from the receiving agent's input, causing it to repeat discovery, lose constraints, or ask again for existing authorization.

content.name: when
content: Task state was available before a context transition and omitted from the continuation that needed it; the maintainer can change the transition policy.

content.name: p
content: On future continuations that receive the preserved state, redundant retrieval, constraint violations, and repeated authorization requests attributable to that omission should decline. Legitimate source refreshes and requests for expanded authority should remain.

content.name: p
content: Failures before any transition should not improve through this mechanism. Persistence despite confirmed delivery weakens the omission explanation; acting beyond preserved permission suggests that the intervention lost its scope restrictions.

content.name: p
content: The context-management system should carry forward the information needed for unfinished work. Its selection or delivery policy instead omits still-applicable evidence, constraints, or authorization at compaction or delegation. A later decision must reconstruct that state or proceeds without it.

content.name: p
content: This is a proposed explanation of the configured system.

content.name: ref
content: Repeated retrieval
alone does not establish it, and a transcript retaining information does not establish that the receiving model had it.

content.name: p
content: Identify a specific fact, constraint, or authorization that was available before the transition and remained applicable to the later decision.

content.name: p
content: The transition output and effective receiving input show the needed state omitted or materially altered, with no equivalent representation available at that decision. Inaccessible model inputs leave this criterion unknown.

attributes.title: A disruption the missing state explains

content.name: p
content: The continuation unnecessarily retrieves the same evidence, violates the omitted constraint, or requests authorization already granted. Identify the connection to the particular missing state rather than relying on timing alone.

content.name: p
content: Information legitimately expired or the user changed the requirement or authorization before continuation.

content.name: p
content: The receiving input contains an adequate equivalent of the necessary state. Poor use of visible information requires another explanation.

content.name: p
content: Compare the original usable result with actual model input before the transition. Backend success or a saved file alone cannot establish prior delivery.

attributes.title: A standing rule demands the behavior

content.name: p
content: Check whether a fresh-consent or repeated-check rule still requires the action when the state is visible. For excessive checking, consider

content.name: ref
content: verification policy overgeneralization

attributes.title: The agent acts against visible state

content.name: p
content: If the relevant state is present and clear at the decision, investigate competing instructions and action selection. Do not infer internal forgetting from incompatible behavior.

content.name: p
content: Inspect the affected transition and the next decision using existing input captures where available. Compare which state survived with what the pending work needed. Look for ordinary continuations under the same policy that preserved the state and proceeded correctly; no replay of the incident is required.

content.name: p
ref
content: Preserve task state across context transitions
changes future handoffs and compactions. A one-time reminder may rescue an episode but does not repair the transition policy.

content.name: p
content: This is an unvalidated working model. The entry supplies neither an adjudicated public case establishing the mechanism nor evidence that the intervention is effective. Evidence for an omission, its contribution to behavior, and benefit from changing the policy are separate claims.

documents.summary: The discovery interface identifies a tool as available without supplying the callable interface needed by the next agent turn, leaving the system searching for a capability it cannot use.
documents.title: Tool discovery delivery gap

content.name: summary
content: The discovery interface identifies a tool as available without supplying the callable interface needed by the next agent turn, leaving the system searching for a capability it cannot use.

content.name: when
content: Discovery is expected to make a tool callable, but registration or delivery to the receiving turn is missing or inconsistent.

content.name: p
content: After the adapter delivers a usable tool or an explicit unavailable result, repeated discovery for that same capability should decline. Available tools should be invoked when the task calls for them; unavailable tools should lead to a supported alternative or a specific blocker.

content.name: p
content: Invocation errors from invalid credentials, bad arguments, or external services may persist. Repeated search despite a confirmed callable interface weakens this diagnosis. Fewer searches accompanied by missing required tool work is not improvement.

content.name: p
content: In a deferred-tool system, discovery must connect a capability name to an invocation contract available to the receiving model and runtime. A partial handoff can advertise success while omitting the schema, registration, or supported invocation route. Rediscovery then returns the same reference without repairing the gap.

content.name: p
content: The problem is the discovery-to-invocation boundary. Repeated search is a clue, not proof that this boundary failed.

content.name: p
content: The adapter's contract says a successful discovery response makes the identified capability callable for the relevant turn.

content.name: p
content: Inspection of registration and effective model input establishes that the required callable interface or supported route was not delivered despite a successful discovery response.

content.name: p
content: The agent needs that capability and enters repeated unsuccessful discovery cycles matching

content.name: ref
content: doom looping
, while those cycles leave the invocation gap unchanged.

content.name: p
content: The service promises only a directory reference and supplies a working, documented next step to activate it.

content.name: p
content: Activation is asynchronous, still within its stated completion window, and the agent is following the supported wait or retry path.

attributes.title: A callable tool is present but unused

content.name: p
content: Inspect the effective tool set for the actual decision turn. A transcript showing only a tool name cannot distinguish this explanation from a delivery gap.

content.name: p
content: Look for an actual invocation and its authentication, permission, argument, or service error. Fixing discovery will not necessarily remove that block.

attributes.title: A later transition removes a delivered interface

content.name: p
content: Establish whether the interface was initially usable and then lost at a transition; that timing distinguishes initial delivery failure from

content.name: ref
content: context handoff loss

content.name: p
content: Compare one failed discovery-to-use sequence with a successful sequence under the same adapter. Inspect the discovery result, registration state, receiving tool definitions, and invocation route. If those inputs are unavailable, retain this as an unconfirmed differential instead of diagnosing from repeated searches.

content.name: p
ref
content: Complete the discovery-to-invocation handoff
repairs the interface used on future turns. A blanket search limit may hide the loop while leaving needed capabilities inaccessible.

content.name: p
content: This is an unvalidated scaffold. No public case in this entry establishes missing registration or model-visible delivery, and no intervention benefit is claimed. It makes no claim about a particular tool provider or harness.

documents.summary: A standing checking policy applies beyond the risks or decisions it was meant to address, producing redundant verification even when the agent follows its instructions.
documents.title: Verification policy overgeneralization

content.name: summary
content: A standing checking policy applies beyond the risks or decisions it was meant to address, producing redundant verification even when the agent follows its instructions.

content.name: when
content: A specific editable instruction or workflow triggers checks without a relevant changed state, unresolved question, or still-unmet acceptance need.

content.name: p
content: After narrowing that rule, verification overrun should decline for the affected class of work while required checks and defect detection remain intact. The reduction should occur at the rule's trigger points, not uniformly across unrelated tasks.

content.name: p
content: Continued extra checks after the revised rule reaches the agent favor another cause. Fewer checks with more missed defects suggest the scope was narrowed too far; slower delivery from another bottleneck may remain.

content.name: p
content: A verification policy should connect each required check to a decision, risk, or acceptance condition and define when enough evidence has been gathered. A broad or self-retriggering rule instead demands another check irrespective of whether the relevant state changed or the question was already answered.

content.name: p
content: The agent may be complying perfectly with that rule. The proposed pathology is in the configured checking policy, not an inference about caution, anxiety, or intent.

attributes.title: An operative rule triggers the work

content.name: p
content: Identify the actual instruction or workflow rule and the decision points where it caused the extra checks. Similar wording in an unused file is insufficient.

attributes.title: The trigger exceeds the checking need

content.name: p
content: Establish that the rule covers a class of work whose relevant verification need is already satisfied or absent. Name the missing justification; elapsed time or passing results alone do not establish waste.

content.name: p
content: Following the rule produces

content.name: ref
content: excessive verification
, with delay or resource use traceable to the extra checks. Equivalent rereads may also match

content.name: ref
content: repeated retrieval

content.name: p
content: The checks address an unmet acceptance condition, relevant risk, new change, or an agreed repeatability study.

content.name: p
content: The chosen check is appropriate but expensive because of its implementation or environment. Slow execution alone does not establish an overgeneral policy.

attributes.title: The system loses evidence that checking finished

content.name: p
content: Inspect whether the prior result reaches the later turn. Repetition after a transition may instead reflect

content.name: ref
content: context handoff loss

content.name: p
content: Compare code, environment, and failures at each trigger. The later check may answer a genuinely new question.

attributes.title: Extra checking is not prescribed by the rule

content.name: p
content: Compare the instruction with the chosen action. If the rule already limits scope and the agent exceeds it, this policy explanation is incomplete.

content.name: p
content: Map extra checks to the rule and the question each result could answer. Include a healthy task where the same rule is useful. Inspect ordinary future work after a scoped policy change; a costly replay study is not a prerequisite.

content.name: p
ref
content: Give verification a scope and stopping condition
changes the offending policy. The maintainer must have authority to change it; an executing agent should not silently bypass a mandatory gate.

content.name: p
content: This is an unvalidated working model. An inefficient-looking check does not by itself establish a bad rule, and the entry provides no measured effect of changing one. Agreement about justified verification may vary with task risk.

documents.summary: The verification workflow promotes a limited check into evidence for a broader acceptance condition, so untested boundaries disappear from completion decisions.
documents.title: Verification scope collapse

content.name: summary
content: The verification workflow promotes a limited check into evidence for a broader acceptance condition, so untested boundaries disappear from completion decisions.

content.name: when
content: The QA skill, tool result, or completion policy treats a component or simulated check as sufficient for a broader required behavior.

content.name: p
content: Future tasks requiring the broader behavior should exercise its actual acceptance path and produce fewer unsupported verification claims. Failures at previously bypassed boundaries may become visible even before underlying implementation quality improves.

content.name: p
content: Component-only tasks should retain their lightweight checks. If claims become narrower but required paths remain untested, the intervention changed reporting without completing the repair. Persistent overclaims despite clear path evidence favor a separate interpretation or reporting failure.

content.name: p
content: Verification evidence has a scope: a component, input path, artifact revision, environment, or physical stage. The system should preserve that scope when deciding whether acceptance has been demonstrated. Instead, its workflow equates a narrower success with the broader requirement and closes the requirement without evidence for the missing boundary.

content.name: p
content: A hypothetical example is treating a successful internal handler call as proof that the user-facing input reaches that handler. The handler may work perfectly while the input path remains unknown.

content.name: p
content: Identify the requested behavior and the boundaries its verification must cover.

content.name: p
content: The actual check bypasses or omits a required boundary, and no independent matching evidence closes that gap.

attributes.title: The workflow promotes the limited result

content.name: p
content: A policy, tool-result transformation, or recorded acceptance decision equates that limited result with satisfaction of the broader condition, producing

content.name: ref
content: unsupported verification claims
. An overclaim with no evidence of this promotion leaves the mechanism unknown.

content.name: p
content: A separate check covers the required path, revision, and environment, including external evidence the local transcript does not contain.

content.name: p
content: The requested work and the report are explicitly limited to the tested component.

attributes.title: The required path was tested and failed

content.name: p
content: Inspect actual inputs and outputs. A real-path defect requires an implementation repair; it does not establish scope collapse unless the workflow substitutes other evidence for the failure.

content.name: p
content: Match revision and destination. Correct testing of an earlier build can produce false assurance without a component-to-whole substitution.

attributes.title: The acceptance boundary is retained but misreported

content.name: p
content: If the workflow leaves the broader condition open and the final report alone claims it passed, investigate reporting. A shared symptom does not establish the same mechanism.

content.name: p
content: Trace one acceptance condition from its task requirement through the executed check, returned result, and completion decision. Identify exactly where scope was broadened. Look for successful work where the real path was exercised without unnecessary additional testing.

content.name: p
ref
content: Verify through the required acceptance path
changes the QA workflow to exercise the missing boundary. Merely softening the final report does not complete an unmet acceptance condition.

content.name: p
content: This is an unvalidated scaffold with a hypothetical illustration. A gap in shown verification supports a symptom more readily than this causal account; unavailable external evidence remains an uncertainty. No efficacy or prevalence claim is made.

documents.summary: Change the compaction or handoff policy to carry still-needed evidence, constraints, and scoped authorization into future receiving inputs.
documents.title: Preserve task state across context transitions

attributes.title: Preserve task state across context transitions

content.name: summary
content: Change the compaction or handoff policy to carry still-needed evidence, constraints, and scoped authorization into future receiving inputs.

content.name: p
content: Repair continuity across context transitions so future agents can use established task state. The intervention changes the transition mechanism or reusable handoff instructions, rather than adding a reminder to one completed incident.

content.name: p
content: Information stored in a transcript or memory file helps only when the receiving agent can use it. Preserve the smallest sufficient state with its source and scope; an excerpt of untrusted data must not become a new instruction.

content.name: p
content: Identify still-needed state that the current transition policy omits, and the class of later decisions it affects. Repetition alone does not establish an omission.

content.name: p
content: The maintainer can change the compaction, delegation, or context-loading policy and has authority to supply the relevant information to the receiving agent.

content.name: p
content: Locate the shared policy that selects and delivers state at the affected transition. Record its current version and the decision-relevant omission.

content.name: p
content: Modify that policy to retain pending decisions, still-applicable constraints, authorization with its limits, and the minimum evidence needed for the next work. Keep source identifiers and freshness conditions; omit completed or irrelevant history.

content.name: p
content: Wire the selected state into the receiving input through the normal handoff or context-loading path. Preserve instruction precedence and source trust. Invalidate evidence when its source changes, and never broaden permissions while summarizing them.

content.name: p
content: Inspect a representative subsequent transition to check that the selected state reaches the receiving input without immediate truncation. If effective input is inaccessible, record delivery as unconfirmed.

content.name: p
content: Observe later tasks with the affected transition. Compare their relevant decisions with the predictions recorded before applying the policy change.

content.name: p
content: Choose a review point with actual opportunities for the omitted state to matter. Track avoidable rediscovery, constraint adherence, and appropriate authorization decisions alongside completion, correctness, and context cost. Compare similar transitions using existing logs; a replay study is optional.

content.name: p
content: Improvement after confirmed delivery supports the relevant diagnosis-dependent prediction. Persistence despite delivery weakens a simple omission account; missing delivery leaves the change untested. Fewer rereads accompanied by stale decisions or fewer permission questions accompanied by unauthorized actions are harmful outcomes.

content.name: p
content: Retained state can become stale, displace useful context, strip permission limits, or promote source text into authority. Changes in task mix, source freshness, and model behavior can also change the symptom rate.

content.name: p
content: Narrow or revert the retention policy if it introduces stale decisions, authorization errors, or excessive context cost. Restore the previous transition configuration and correct affected retained state; reverting cannot undo actions already taken.

content.name: p
content: This is a proposed system change with no efficacy result established here. Successful storage, successful delivery, and improved decisions are separate claims.

documents.summary: Replace an overbroad checking instruction with a rule that specifies its trigger, required coverage, completion condition, and reasons to reopen verification.
documents.title: Give verification a scope and stopping condition

attributes.title: Give verification a scope and stopping condition

content.name: summary
content: Replace an overbroad checking instruction with a rule that specifies its trigger, required coverage, completion condition, and reasons to reopen verification.

content.name: p
content: Reduce redundant checking by fixing the policy that generates it. Verification should answer a task-relevant question; more passing runs do not necessarily add evidence. Retain checks justified by the work's risks and acceptance conditions.

content.name: p
content: A specific instruction or workflow causes extra checks, and the maintainer can identify the class of work for which its scope is excessive.

content.name: p
content: The maintainer has authority to revise that policy and can identify the requirements that must remain enforced. Otherwise seek the policy owner's change rather than bypassing it during execution.

content.name: p
content: Identify the decision or failure risk the rule is intended to address and the checks needed to address it.

content.name: p
content: Edit the source instruction or workflow to state when it applies, which relevant checks satisfy it, and when checking stops. State the changes or new failures that warrant reopening it. Remove conflicting blanket instructions in the same policy.

content.name: p
content: Retain mandatory coverage and justified repeated sampling. For example, a targeted check may finish a small local edit while release approval still requires the project's release gate; neither is automatically a substitute for the other.

content.name: p
content: Deliver the revised policy to future agents and confirm it is active at an affected decision. Review subsequent eligible work for both reduced overrun and preserved defect detection.

content.name: p
content: Before the change, predict which trigger points should lose redundant work and which checks should remain. At a proportionate review point, compare time spent after requirements were satisfied, checks repeated without new justification, missed defects, and usable task completion in comparable work.

content.name: p
content: Less checking alone is insufficient. If defects rise, coverage may have been removed. If the revised rule reaches the agent but excess checking persists, inspect other instructions and decision behavior. Work with no relevant check opportunity supplies little evidence.

content.name: p
content: A narrow rule can miss interacting changes or encourage premature completion. A different task mix or faster test infrastructure can also reduce checking time without validating the policy explanation.

content.name: p
content: Restore needed coverage if the change skips required gates or misses relevant defects. Revert the rule or narrow its exception; preserve evidence of defects and repair affected artifacts separately.

content.name: p
content: This intervention is unvalidated. Its usefulness depends on correctly identifying an overbroad rule; it is not a general recommendation to test less.

documents.summary: Change the reusable QA workflow so acceptance checks exercise the required input-to-result path on the relevant artifact, while component checks retain their actual scope.
documents.title: Verify through the required acceptance path

attributes.title: Verify through the required acceptance path

content.name: summary
content: Change the reusable QA workflow so acceptance checks exercise the required input-to-result path on the relevant artifact, while component checks retain their actual scope.

content.name: p
content: Make future verification cover the boundary that matters to the task. A component probe can help locate a defect without proving that a user's input, deployment path, or physical process reaches that component correctly.

content.name: p
content: Identify a required acceptance boundary omitted by the current QA workflow and the relevant artifact or destination.

content.name: p
content: The maintainer can change the QA skill, template, or harness, and the needed check is feasible within the task's access, cost, and authorization limits. Otherwise preserve the unresolved requirement rather than claiming verification.

content.name: p
content: Update the reusable QA instructions to connect the relevant acceptance condition to its input, artifact version, and observable result. Select the smallest check that covers that path.

content.name: p
content: Change the default acceptance procedure to use the required interface. For a user-input requirement, drive that input rather than calling its internal handler; for a delivered artifact, inspect the relevant destination. Wait for asynchronous completion using its observable result and an appropriate timeout.

content.name: p
content: Keep component probes available for diagnosis, but label their results with what they exercised. Do not let a component success close a broader acceptance condition without matching evidence. Use existing check output; a new receipt format is not required.

content.name: p
content: Confirm subsequent QA work follows the revised path and review both acceptance outcomes and the accuracy of claims based on them.

content.name: p
content: Predict which previously bypassed failures may become visible and which component-only tasks should remain unchanged. On future applicable work, inspect whether the required path was attempted, whether it worked, and whether the final statement matches the result. Record blocked or unavailable checks as unresolved.

content.name: p
content: Fewer overclaims with the required path still untested is only a reporting improvement. Newly detected defects may mean the check became more informative, not that implementation quality deteriorated. Persistent real-path failures require their own repair.

content.name: p
content: Full paths can be slow, flaky, or have external effects. Restrict the procedure to the task's actual acceptance boundary and authorized environment; do not require live deployment or physical fabrication for every component change.

content.name: p
content: Narrow or revert a check that introduces unauthorized effects, false blocking, or disproportionate delay. Keep the broader condition open when coverage is removed; rollback does not turn missing evidence into a pass.

content.name: p
content: This is an unvalidated workflow change. Better verification may reveal defects without fixing them, and a more accurate report alone does not establish better task completion.

documents.summary: Change the collection and publication path so source observations, authorized calculations, and missing values remain distinguishable in future outputs.
documents.title: Keep derived values out of source-only fields

attributes.title: Keep derived values out of source-only fields

content.name: summary
content: Change the collection and publication path so source observations, authorized calculations, and missing values remain distinguishable in future outputs.

content.name: p
content: Prevent

content.name: ref
content: inferred values presented as observations
by preserving a field's meaning through collection and serialization. An accurate calculation can still violate a source-only contract.

content.name: p
content: The task or output format distinguishes source-reported fields from calculations, and that distinction is being lost or bypassed.

content.name: p
content: The maintainer can change the collector instructions, serializer, or publication template and its consumers without silently changing the agreed output contract.

content.name: p
content: Update the reusable collector and serializer to keep an observed value tied to its source location. Permit calculations only in explicitly authorized derived fields, with their formula and inputs; preserve the contract's missing-value representation.

content.name: p
content: Remove formula fallbacks and guessed defaults from source-only assignments. When the source lacks a value, publish the agreed missing marker rather than a computed substitute. If the current format cannot express the distinction, leave that field missing and report the limitation.

content.name: p
content: Check the final publication path with one observed value, a genuine zero, a missing value, and an authorized calculation. Confirm that serialization and display retain each meaning; use the existing data model where it can express these distinctions.

content.name: p
content: Review subsequent comparable outputs against available source evidence, including outputs that look complete and those with missing fields.

content.name: p
content: Predict fewer unsupported non-missing values in source-only fields, with genuine observations and permitted calculations preserved. Compare published values with accessible sources and inspect whether downstream consumers retain the distinction.

content.name: p
content: More missing values may reflect honest uncertainty, lost access, or a broken collector. Check useful data coverage and publication success alongside provenance accuracy. Correct source records with misleading rendered labels point to the publication layer; this change will not repair unrelated date filters or arithmetic errors.

content.name: p
content: Overstrict handling can discard valid observations, convert real zeros to missing values, or break consumers expecting a complete row. Source changes and inaccessible source pages limit retrospective assessment.

content.name: p
content: Repair or revert the faulty collector or serializer if valid data is lost or publication breaks. Preserve the observed-versus-derived distinction in a compatible output or an explicit limitation; do not reinstate silent fabrication as the fallback.

content.name: p
content: This proposed intervention has no established outcome here. It can be appropriate from an observed contract violation without a catalog diagnosis; the underlying cause may lie in instructions, extraction, serialization, or presentation.

documents.summary: Change the deferred-tool adapter so successful discovery delivers a callable interface to the receiving turn, and failed activation returns an explicit unavailable result.
documents.title: Complete the discovery-to-invocation handoff

content.name: summary
content: Change the deferred-tool adapter so successful discovery delivers a callable interface to the receiving turn, and failed activation returns an explicit unavailable result.

content.name: p
content: Repair the interface between tool discovery and use. A capability name is not enough when invocation requires additional schema or runtime registration. Discovery should either complete that handoff or tell the agent what remains blocked.

content.name: p
content: The adapter promises callable access after discovery, but inspection shows a gap in registration, schema delivery, or the supported invocation route.

content.name: p
content: The maintainer can change and inspect the adapter and receiving tool configuration while preserving existing permissions.

content.name: p
content: Locate where discovery resolves the capability, where runtime registration occurs, and how the receiving turn gets its invocation contract.

content.name: p
content: Change that shared path to register and deliver the interface before reporting callable availability. If activation is asynchronous, return its pending state and supported continuation instead of an apparently completed discovery.

content.name: p
content: Return an explicit unavailable result when activation fails, with the actionable reason and supported recovery if one exists. Repeated discovery should not return the same success-looking reference while the capability remains inaccessible.

content.name: p
content: Inspect a representative receiving input and safe invocation, then observe ordinary subsequent tool-use opportunities. Check an unavailable capability as well so errors remain visible and permission boundaries hold.

content.name: p
content: Record predictions for available and unavailable tools separately. On applicable future turns, compare successful discovery-to-use transitions, repeated searches for the same capability, explicit blocks, and completed required tool work.

content.name: p
content: Confirmed delivery with continued rediscovery weakens the delivery-gap explanation. Correct invocations that fail at an external service indicate another obstruction. Fewer searches caused by silently skipping required work are not success.

content.name: p
content: Loading unnecessary schemas can consume context; stale registrations can call the wrong interface. Adapter changes must preserve authorization and tool selection. Model or provider changes can independently affect discovery behavior.

content.name: p
content: Revert the adapter change if it exposes unauthorized tools, delivers incompatible schemas, or breaks working routes. Report unavailable capabilities explicitly while repairing the handoff; do not mask activation failures as successful access.

content.name: p
content: This is an unvalidated proposed adapter repair. No particular harness is asserted to have this defect, and a completed handoff does not guarantee correct tool choice or successful task completion.

documents.summary: An agent retrieves already-delivered information again without a new content, freshness, or verification need.
documents.title: Repeated retrieval

content.name: summary
content: An agent retrieves already-delivered information again without a new content, freshness, or verification need.

content.name: p
content: Within one task episode, the agent retrieves substantially the same information again after an earlier usable result was delivered, for at least two retrievals in total. The later retrieval supplies no needed new content or source state and addresses no unmet freshness or verification need; a standing instruction to reread does not by itself establish such a need.

content.name: p
content: In the session transcript or tool audit log, group retrievals by the question answered, source, and returned passage or field. Compare result bodies or hashes, delivery status, and file versions or timestamps; identical commands can return changed content, while different commands can return the same content.

content.name: p
content: Check task requirements, source-change risks, and intervening edits for a new content need, freshness condition, or unresolved verification question. Pair each candidate repeat with the earlier delivered result, and use context snapshots or compaction summaries to investigate whether that result remained available at the later call. A rule can explain a redundant read without making it useful; record that rule for investigation.

content.name: p
content: A reread after an edit returns the changed setting needed for the next decision. Unlike

content.name: ref
content: multi-read
, it supplies a needed new source state.

content.name: p
content: A second call obtains a different passage or field needed for the task. It does not retrieve substantially the same information as

content.name: ref
content: multi-read

content.name: p
content: A retry obtains information whose earlier result was empty, wrong, truncated before the needed content, or not delivered. The earlier usable delivery required by

content.name: ref
content: multi-read
is absent. This excludes this symptom, not a delivery fault or

content.name: ref
content: doom looping
if repeated unsuccessful retries meet its definition.

content.name: p
content: A reading at a decision boundary establishes freshness needed for a decision about mutable state, even if the value is unchanged. It answers an unmet freshness need, unlike

content.name: ref
content: multi-read
; a generic reread instruction alone is insufficient.

content.name: p
content: An independent second retrieval checks a still-unresolved reliability question, and the agent performs that check. It supplies verification evidence missing from

content.name: ref
content: multi-read
; equivalent repetitions after the question is settled are not excluded merely because a rule demands them.

content.name: p
content: Record the episode identifier and date, task type, model and harness versions, retrieval tools, and relevant instructions. Preserve call timestamps, arguments, source versions, returned passages or permitted hashes, delivery status, and the earlier result associated with each repeat. Include total retrievals and repeat counts, output volume, elapsed time, tokens or cost where available, context transitions, intervening edits, and the eventual task outcome. Record user interruptions and recovery work so incident frequency and impact can be compared across runs.

content.name: p
content: Synthetic incident: an agent reads a 200-line configuration file, extracts the requested setting, and rereads the unchanged file twice without making the edit or encountering a new requirement. The tool log and file hash identify two redundant retrievals: 400 additional lines enter the transcript while the edit remains unstarted.

content.name: p
content: Synthetic comparison: an agent reads a configuration file, edits one setting, and rereads it once. The diff and returned value show that the second read verifies the changed state; two reads support one completed edit and reveal no redundant retrieval under this definition.

content.name: p
content: Reported incident:

content.name: a
content: Claude Code issue #59318

describes recognizing 30–50+ consecutive grep calls with identical arguments and output during codebase research. The reporter says tasks expected to take 2–3 minutes instead occupied 1–2 hours and required manual interruption. The account supplies repetition and impact estimates, but not a complete trace separating model requests from runtime replays.

documents.summary: An agent repeats an unsuccessful action cycle without relevant changes that would reasonably support expecting a different outcome.
documents.title: Doom looping

content.name: summary
content: An agent repeats an unsuccessful action cycle without relevant changes that would reasonably support expecting a different outcome.

content.name: p
content: Within one task episode, at least three consecutive complete action-and-feedback cycles aimed at the same immediate outcome fail to advance it. Across those cycles, there is no evidenced change in relevant inputs, environment, available information, or strategy sufficient to justify expecting a different result.

content.name: p
content: Use the session transcript and tool execution log to pair attempts with their feedback, such as an edit with its test result or a search with its returned matches. Group cycles by the immediate outcome; this helps separate several tool calls within one attempt from successive attempts.

content.name: p
content: Compare command arguments, outputs, file diffs, service status, and timestamps between cycles. Look for evidence that a retry addresses the blocker: a corrected credential, new error, eliminated hypothesis, or documented recovery interval. Mark gaps in the recorded state rather than filling them with an assumption that nothing changed.

content.name: p
content: Retries follow a documented transient failure and a recovery interval that gives the next attempt a reason to succeed. That changed recovery state differs from

content.name: ref
content: stalled cycles
; a retry limit alone would not explain unchanged failures.

content.name: p
content: Status checks follow an active external job at its expected cadence, and job telemetry shows progress or a documented completion window. The evolving job state supplies the relevant change missing from

content.name: ref
content: stalled cycles

content.name: p
content: Successive attempts eliminate distinct hypotheses or add samples to a planned stochastic estimate. They advance the immediate investigation or add relevant information, unlike

content.name: ref
content: stalled cycles

content.name: p
content: Record the episode identifier and date, model and harness versions, task type, immediate outcome, and the action/feedback boundaries used to count cycles. Preserve requested and executed calls, feedback, relevant state changes, retry policy, and context transitions. Include total cycles, consecutive stalled cycles, elapsed time, tokens or cost where available, and how the sequence ended: recovery, automatic limit, user interruption, or abandonment. Retain the corpus revision and actual counts so the provisional three-cycle screening rule can be reassessed across incidents.

content.name: p
content: Synthetic incident: five file-read attempts receive permission denied over two minutes. The trace shows only quoting and output-format changes; credentials and access rights stay unchanged. Comparing the five errors exposes five stalled cycles, two minutes of delay, and no retrieved file before the user interrupts.

content.name: p
content: Reported incident:

content.name: a
content: Claude Code issue #59318

describes 30–50+ identical grep calls returning identical output before manual interruption. The reporter recognized the loop in the repeated commands and estimated 1–2 hours spent on research expected to take 2–3 minutes. A complete execution trace is not supplied, so responsibility for the repeats remains unresolved.

content.name: p
content: Synthetic comparison: five successive edits resolve five different test failures. Test logs show the remaining failure count falling from five to zero. Although the agent repeats the edit/test cycle five times, each cycle advances the outcome and the final suite passes.

documents.summary: An agent shows an abrupt, observable decline relative to its own recent performance on comparable work.
documents.title: Sudden performance degradation

content.name: summary
content: An agent shows an abrupt, observable decline relative to its own recent performance on comparable work.

content.name: p
content: After a bounded transition, at least two consecutive comparable outputs or task attempts perform worse on a named measure than a recorded recent baseline under the same acceptance criteria. The decline appears as errors, missed requirements, reduced completion, or greater time or cost for an equivalent accepted result.

content.name: p
content: Locate the last adequate and first degraded work in session transcripts, saved outputs, evaluation results, or issue history. Put the before-and-after artifacts beside the acceptance criteria and compare the named measure, task difficulty, and available information.

content.name: p
content: Use timestamps and model/client release records to locate the transition, then inspect tool logs, memory files, handoff summaries, and configuration changes for differences worth investigating. Preserve successful as well as failed nearby attempts so the baseline and the extent of the decline can be checked.

content.name: p
content: Later work requires substantially different skills or complexity. It lacks the comparable tasks required by

content.name: ref
content: performance drop
, even if its raw success rate is lower.

content.name: p
content: The user changes acceptance criteria or explicitly requests a faster, cheaper result with lower quality. The before-and-after work is not assessed under the same criteria as

content.name: ref
content: performance drop

content.name: p
content: One failed attempt occurs among otherwise comparable successes, with the next attempt returning to baseline. It does not meet the two consecutive degraded attempts in

content.name: ref
content: performance drop

content.name: p
content: Record the episode or run identifiers, dates, task types, model/client and harness versions, effort settings, and the performance measure with its units. Preserve baseline and later artifacts, acceptance criteria, sample sizes, successful and failed attempts, and the transition interval. Include task difficulty, context transitions, tool availability, configuration or service changes, completion rates, latency, cost, and user rework where available. Keep the corpus revision and raw comparisons so the two-attempt screening rule and apparent trends can be reassessed.

content.name: p
content: Synthetic incident: an agent produces six valid records under a four-field rule, then omits two fields from each of the next six comparable records after resuming the session. Comparing outputs with the unchanged schema reveals a fall from 6/6 valid records to 0/6 and twelve missing values requiring repair. The timing identifies a transition, not its cause.

content.name: p
content: Reported investigation:

content.name: a
content: Anthropic’s April 23, 2026 postmortem

describes a prompt change that reduced coding quality. Broader evaluations and prompt ablations exposed a reported 3% drop on one evaluation for Opus 4.6 and 4.7, leading to a rollback. A separate resumed-session bug produced forgetfulness, repetition, and faster usage-limit depletion. These are population-level comparisons; the postmortem does not publish the consecutive task results needed to adjudicate a particular episode under this screening rule.

content.name: p
content: Synthetic comparison: an agent completes five typo fixes and fails one distributed-systems redesign. The task records reveal a change in difficulty and only one failed redesign, so the five successes and one failure do not establish this symptom or quantify a decline on comparable work.

documents.summary: An agent continues or expands verification beyond the task’s justified checking needs, delaying the requested outcome.
documents.title: Excessive verification

content.name: summary
content: An agent continues or expands verification beyond the task’s justified checking needs, delaying the requested outcome.

content.name: p
content: Verification continues or additional checking work is created after an applicable stopping condition has been met, beyond an explicit verification scope or budget, or through repeated equivalent checks without a relevant change or unresolved question. The extra work delays delivery or consumes resources without an unmet acceptance need, relevant risk, or investigation question that justifies it; an overbroad standing rule can cause this behavior.

content.name: p
content: Start with the user request, project instructions, release rules, and any agreed checking budget or stopping condition. Build a timeline from test commands, CI runs, background jobs, and their results, marking when the requested checks were satisfied.

content.name: p
content: Compare later checks against code and environment changes, unresolved failures, and the decisions their results informed. Inspect diffs for newly created test infrastructure and job logs for setup or repair time. Distinguish a rule's existence from the acceptance need or risk it addresses; new failures, unmet coverage, and planned repeatability studies can justify further checking.

content.name: p
content: A release, security, or project check supplies coverage still needed for the requested action. That unmet acceptance need distinguishes it from

content.name: ref
content: checking overrun
, even when the suite takes longer than the edit. A policy requiring equivalent checks after that need is met may itself warrant diagnosis.

content.name: p
content: A check reveals a relevant new failure or an edit affects additional behavior. The new evidence justifies the broader checking, unlike the unexplained extra work in

content.name: ref
content: checking overrun

content.name: p
content: Unchanged runs belong to an agreed flakiness, load, or reproducibility investigation. They answer its unresolved question and satisfy its checking scope, so repetition alone is not

content.name: ref
content: checking overrun

content.name: p
content: Record the episode identifier and date, task type, model and harness versions, requested outcome and urgency, explicit checking budget, mandatory gates, and stopping condition. Preserve check commands, selected tests, job timestamps, state changes, results, and the decision each check informed. Include required versus unexplained runs, infrastructure added, time after the stopping condition, tokens or cost where available, delivery delay, and defects actually caught. Record total tasks or checks reviewed when aggregating incidents, rather than treating a count of complaints as a rate.

content.name: p
content: Synthetic incident: a user requests a reversible text edit and one targeted check, which passes. With no new failure or broader requirement, the agent installs a test framework, repairs its setup, and runs the full suite twice. The command timeline shows twenty-four additional minutes before delivery and no further defect found.

content.name: p
content: Reported incident:

content.name: a
content: a Claude Code user reports repeated runs of more than 1,500 tests after small edits despite instructions to stop

. The user recognized the activity by inspecting long-running background tasks and reports about two hours per run, with the project largely stalled for weeks. These are user estimates; the post does not supply a full trace establishing the applicable requirements for each run.

content.name: p
content: Synthetic comparison: a one-line authentication edit takes one minute and its mandatory regression suite takes twelve minutes. The release policy and CI log account for the longer check; the run satisfies a required gate rather than adding unexplained verification.

documents.summary: An agent acknowledges a specific correction and then repeats the corrected behavior under comparable conditions.
documents.title: Correction without behavioral change

content.name: summary
content: An agent acknowledges a specific correction and then repeats the corrected behavior under comparable conditions.

content.name: p
content: After receiving and acknowledging an applicable correction, the agent performs materially the same corrected action at least once more while that correction remains in force. The acknowledgment and later action are both observable in the episode or linked continuation.

content.name: p
content: In the transcript, pair the specific correction and acknowledgment with the next relevant tool call, edit, or answer. Use execution timestamps to distinguish a newly chosen action from one already in flight, and compare intervening instructions for a change in scope.

content.name: p
content: Inspect saved feedback files, memory loading records, and handoff summaries alongside the later input where available. These can show what was retained or omitted; compare actual later actions with the correction rather than treating an apology or memory write as proof of compliance.

content.name: p
content: The later action falls outside the correction’s stated scope. It therefore lacks the applicable correction required by

content.name: ref
content: repeated violation

content.name: p
content: A later applicable instruction changes the rule, or a higher-priority requirement displaces it. The original correction is no longer in force as required by

content.name: ref
content: repeated violation

content.name: p
content: Execution logs show that the apparent recurrence was issued before the correction and acknowledgment. It is not a later action chosen after acknowledgment under

content.name: ref
content: repeated violation

content.name: p
content: Record the episode identifier and date, task type, model/harness versions, the correction’s exact text and scope, its delivery and acknowledgment times, and each subsequent opportunity to apply it. Preserve later actions, intervening instructions, memory artifacts, and effective input where available. Include recurrence counts relative to relevant opportunities, user correction turns, elapsed delay, damaged or redone work, and whether behavior eventually changed. Distinguish missing context evidence from a demonstrated loss of the correction.

content.name: p
content: Synthetic incident: after being told to edit a source template rather than generated output, the agent acknowledges the correction but makes the next fix in the generated file. Comparing the correction with the diff identifies the recurrence. The next build overwrites that fix, leaving one unresolved defect and ten minutes of rework.

content.name: p
content: Reported incident:

content.name: a
content: Claude Code issue #37847

lists eight shell-command recurrences after feedback was saved: four Python, two shell-loop, and two Node examples. The reporter compared saved memory and acknowledgments with later commands, describing repeated corrections and lost confidence in memory. Total time lost and the effective input to every invocation are not supplied.

content.name: p
content: Synthetic comparison: after prohibiting edits to generated output, the user explicitly approves one emergency edit there. The transcript records that exception before the single edit, so the change does not violate a correction that remained in force for that action.

documents.summary: A previously established task requirement or decision ceases to govern the agent’s later continuation.
documents.title: Lost task constraints

content.name: summary
content: A previously established task requirement or decision ceases to govern the agent’s later continuation.

content.name: p
content: An explicit, still-applicable task constraint is represented or followed earlier, but a later continuation omits, contradicts, or replaces it and proceeds incompatibly with the original requirement.

content.name: p
content: Find the original requirement and the earlier plan, answer, or action that represented or followed it. Compare those records with later tool calls and artifact diffs to locate the first incompatible continuation.

content.name: p
content: Inspect compaction summaries, handoff messages, memory files, and replacement prompts around that point. Compare them with later user approvals or revisions, and inspect actual execution when a shortened summary leaves a requirement unstated.

content.name: p
content: The user changes or withdraws the earlier constraint before the later action. It is no longer the still-applicable requirement in

content.name: ref
content: constraint loss

content.name: p
content: A shortened summary omits a detail, but later actions still honor it. The incompatible continuation required by

content.name: ref
content: constraint loss
is absent.

content.name: p
content: The agent obtains an authorized resolution to conflicting or infeasible instructions before acting. The later work follows the resolved requirement rather than contradicting a still-applicable one under

content.name: ref
content: constraint loss

content.name: p
content: Record the episode identifier and date, task type, model and harness versions, original requirement and authority, and earlier evidence that it was represented or followed. Preserve later summaries, effective inputs, actions, and the first incompatible result, with compaction or handoff times and superseding instructions. Include the number of established constraints and affected constraints, unauthorized actions, user interruptions, rollback or rework time, and final outcome. Distinguish a missing representation from incompatible behavior when grouping incidents.

content.name: p
content: Synthetic incident: an initial migration plan requires review before execution; a handoff summary instead directs execution. Audit logs show three tables changed before any approval. Comparing the two plans and execution timestamps exposes the lost gate; the user interrupts and spends twelve minutes rolling back the migration.

content.name: p
content: Reported incident:

content.name: a
content: Claude Code issue #23776

compares a request to revise and present a plan with a compaction summary directing implementation. The agent reportedly made multiple file edits, added a test file, and ran builds before review. The user had to interrupt and restate the request; rollback was a possible consequence, not a confirmed outcome. No rework duration is reported.

content.name: p
content: Synthetic comparison: the user reviews a migration and approves execution before the agent runs it. The approval timestamp explains why the next summary omits the completed gate; one authorized migration proceeds without loss of the still-applicable requirements.

documents.summary: An agent ends its turn or run with authorized, actionable work remaining and no identified dependency requiring a stop.
documents.title: Premature stopping

content.name: summary
content: An agent ends its turn or run with authorized, actionable work remaining and no identified dependency requiring a stop.

content.name: p
content: The agent yields a final or idle state while the active request remains incomplete and at least one relevant next step is available within its authority. It does not identify a genuine blocker, requested pause, or completed stopping condition.

content.name: p
content: Compare the active request and acceptance checklist with delivered files, deployed state, or other outputs. Use conversation end markers and scheduler or job status to locate the actual stop and identify a remaining action supported by the available tools and authority.

content.name: p
content: Inspect permission records, missing-input messages, runtime limits, and active background jobs for a dependency that explains the pause. If a later continuation exists, compare its prompt and first action with the stopped state to see whether new information or authorization was supplied.

content.name: p
content: Every relevant next step depends on an approval, credential, choice, or missing input that only the user can provide. The available authorized next step required by

content.name: ref
content: unfinished stop
is absent.

content.name: p
content: A relevant background operation remains active and the system is waiting for its result. The run has not entered the final or idle state described in

content.name: ref
content: unfinished stop

content.name: p
content: The requested stage or agreed budget is complete, or a runtime limit leaves no available next action. A satisfied stopping condition or unavailable continuation excludes these cases from

content.name: ref
content: unfinished stop

content.name: p
content: Record the episode identifier and date, task type, model/client and harness versions, requested acceptance criteria, completed and remaining work, and the concrete next step available at the stop. Preserve the final message, stop reason, tool/job states, runtime limits, and context transitions. Include stop and resume times, unnecessary stops per task, user nudges, unattended waiting time, eventual completion, and abandoned work. Retain the exact resuming prompt to distinguish continuation from new authorization or missing information.

content.name: p
content: Synthetic incident: asked to implement and document a change, the agent implements it and ends by offering to write the documentation. The task checklist and scheduler show one unfinished deliverable and no active job or missing input. The user returns thirty minutes later and says continue; the agent writes the docs, after one unnecessary prompt and thirty minutes of idle delay.

content.name: p
content: Reported incident:

content.name: a
content: Codex issue #33398

describes a generic readiness response ending a turn after a context transition while the original task remained unfinished. The reporter recognized the stop by the ended turn and the need for another message to resume. The reported impact is extra supervision of long-running tasks; stop frequency and waiting duration are not quantified, and the underlying cause remains unresolved.

content.name: p
content: Synthetic comparison: the next authorized stage requires publishing to one of two accounts, and no account has been selected. The request and account list reveal the missing choice. One user reply resolves a genuine dependency, so that pause is not an unnecessary stop.

documents.summary: An agent requests permission again for an action that remains covered by a clear, applicable authorization.
documents.title: Repeated reauthorization

content.name: summary
content: An agent requests permission again for an action that remains covered by a clear, applicable authorization.

content.name: p
content: After explicit, applicable authorization of an action, the agent asks the user to authorize materially the same action at least once more. No changed target, scope, consequence, unmet consent condition, or governing requirement makes renewed approval necessary.

content.name: p
content: Pair each permission question in the transcript with the earlier approval and the proposed tool action. Compare account, resource, recipient, operation, conditions, and timestamps to see whether the approval covers the later action.

content.name: p
content: Check tool permission events, session expiry, and governing instructions for a new gate. Use message provenance to distinguish a conversational question generated by the agent from an enforced platform prompt, and inspect whether an answer led to execution or another question.

content.name: p
content: The operation now affects a different account, recipient, resource, or materially broader scope. It is not the same authorized action required by

content.name: ref
content: redundant permission

content.name: p
content: A governing instruction or tool gate requires fresh approval at this stage or after expiry. This is the renewed-approval requirement excluded by

content.name: ref
content: redundant permission

content.name: p
content: Earlier consent depended on an unmet or unverified condition. That consent is not yet applicable to the action, unlike the authorization in

content.name: ref
content: redundant permission

content.name: p
content: Record the episode identifier and date, task type, model/client and harness versions, original approval text, scope, conditions, and each later permission request. Preserve proposed actions, prompt origin, applicable gate policies, changed circumstances, and expiry or context boundaries. Include authorized actions attempted, redundant requests, user reply counts, approval-to-execution delay, unattended waiting time, and whether the task eventually ran or was abandoned.

content.name: p
content: Synthetic incident: the user approves clicking Continue on a named screen, but the agent asks twice more before clicking. The transcript, unchanged screen, and permission log show no new gate. Two extra replies are required and the click is delayed twelve minutes while the user is away.

content.name: p
content: Reported incident:

content.name: a
content: Codex issue #48998

describes a conversational request to click Continue after that same action had already been approved. The reporter identifies the repeat by comparing the approval with the later question and says authorized unattended work stopped for another reply. The issue does not include the full transcript or a complete policy audit; total blocked time is not quantified.

content.name: p
content: Synthetic comparison: the user approves sending a draft to one colleague, then a proposed action targets a mailing list. Comparing recipient lists exposes the changed scope. One new approval concerns a different action rather than repeating permission for the original send.

documents.summary: An agent modifies artifacts or system state beyond the authorized task scope without an established dependency that requires the change.
documents.title: Unrequested changes

content.name: summary
content: An agent modifies artifacts or system state beyond the authorized task scope without an established dependency that requires the change.

content.name: p
content: The agent makes a material change to an artifact or system state that is outside the requested or otherwise authorized scope and is not supported as necessary to complete the task. This includes reverting unrelated work, unsolicited rewrites, and additional infrastructure.

content.name: p
content: Compare the request and standing instructions with version-control diffs, file snapshots, deployment events, or service audit logs. Identify what the agent actually changed and use timestamps or authorship records to separate its edits from concurrent work.

content.name: p
content: Trace each candidate extra change to the requested behavior using interfaces, dependencies, and configuration. Compare semantic diffs with whitespace-insensitive views, and inspect command results to distinguish a proposed change from an applied one. These records can expose authorized supporting work as well as unrelated cleanup.

content.name: p
content: The requested behavior requires a supporting schema, interface, or configuration change within the granted authority. This is the necessary dependency excluded by

content.name: ref
content: scope expansion

content.name: p
content: The user grants refactoring or cleanup scope that includes the affected components. The change is not outside the authorized boundary in

content.name: ref
content: scope expansion

content.name: p
content: A viewer renders an apparent rewrite, but the underlying artifact and behavior are unchanged. There is no material change under

content.name: ref
content: scope expansion
; actual unsolicited formatting changes still require a scope assessment.

content.name: p
content: Record the episode identifier and date, task type, model and harness versions, request and standing authority, baseline revision, and before-and-after artifacts. Preserve semantic diffs, commands and execution times, claimed dependencies, concurrent-edit ownership, and whether each change was proposed or applied. Include total and out-of-scope files or resources changed, lost work, rollback success, recovery time, downstream failures, and the final task outcome.

content.name: p
content: Synthetic incident: while fixing a parser, the agent restores an unrelated documentation file to HEAD, deleting eighty uncommitted lines written by the user. The pre-run snapshot and reset command identify the deleted work and its lack of connection to the parser. The user spends twenty-five minutes recovering and reapplying the edits.

content.name: p
content: Reported incident:

content.name: a
content: Codex issue #6187

describes unrelated concurrent edits disappearing during the agent’s unexpected-changes check despite instructions to preserve them. The reporter recognizes the resets by comparing work in other files before and after the task and says some incidents erased hours of uncommitted work. Exact recovery time and an independently reproduced trace are not provided.

content.name: p
content: Synthetic comparison: an authorized API field requires edits to a handler, serializer, and schema. Comparing the three-file diff with the API contract explains all three changes, including two files not named in the request; no unrelated work is altered.

documents.summary: An agent claims that requested work is complete while the delivered artifact or resulting state demonstrably lacks a required part.
documents.title: Completion–artifact mismatch

content.name: summary
content: An agent claims that requested work is complete while the delivered artifact or resulting state demonstrably lacks a required part.

content.name: p
content: A completion claim covers a stated deliverable or acceptance criterion, but inspection of the corresponding artifact or system state at that time contradicts the claim. The discrepancy is about delivered work, not merely confidence or phrasing.

content.name: p
content: Take the exact completion statement from the transcript and map it to the requested deliverable. Inspect the named branch, revision, destination, or deployed environment using files, git history, deployment records, or the delivered workflow.

content.name: p
content: Compare artifact timestamps with the claim, and follow persistence, commit, transfer, and deployment events to locate where work stopped reaching the destination. Check disclosed limitations and later modifications before attributing a discrepancy to the state at claim time.

content.name: p
content: The agent accurately reports completion of one stage and identifies unfinished stages. Inspection does not contradict that scoped claim as required by

content.name: ref
content: unsupported completion

content.name: p
content: The reviewer inspects a different revision or destination from the correctly reported one. The corresponding artifact required for

content.name: ref
content: unsupported completion
has not been shown to contradict the claim.

content.name: p
content: The artifact satisfied the reported scope and was changed or removed afterward. There is no contradiction at claim time under

content.name: ref
content: unsupported completion

content.name: p
content: Record the episode identifier and date, task type, model and harness versions, acceptance criteria, exact completion language, and claim time. Preserve artifact identity and revision, inspection steps and results, tool responses, persistence/commit/deployment events, and later modifications. Include claimed versus delivered requirements, time until discovery, failed downstream actions, user reliance on the claim, and repair or rework time. Record accurately disclosed limitations separately from contradicted claims.

content.name: p
content: Synthetic incident: an agent reports that CSV export is implemented and ready. The delivered revision has a button and success message but no export path; exercising that workflow produces zero files. The user discovers the mismatch during a scheduled export and spends twenty minutes producing the CSV manually.

content.name: p
content: Reported incident:

content.name: a
content: Matthew Hawthorne’s February 2026 account

describes a seven-turn resumed task declaring success on a branch with no changes. Code review exposed the empty branch; the earlier run’s uncommitted work had not reached the new worktree. The requested feature was absent despite the completion report, and investigation prompted changes to resume and persistence handling. Recovery time is not given.

content.name: p
content: Synthetic comparison: an agent delivers an export button and explicitly says CSV generation remains unfinished. The diff and a workflow check confirm that exact boundary. One requirement remains open, but the report does not falsely describe it as complete.

documents.summary: An agent reports verification with a result, scope, freshness, or attribution that the available execution evidence does not support.
documents.title: Unsupported verification claims

content.name: summary
content: An agent reports verification with a result, scope, freshness, or attribution that the available execution evidence does not support.

content.name: p
content: The agent states that a check was performed or produced a particular result, but the corresponding execution record contradicts the claim or is demonstrably insufficient for its stated scope. Examples include stale output presented as fresh, a partial run described as a complete suite, and an incorrectly attributed failure.

content.name: p
content: Extract verification statements from final messages, pull-request descriptions, or status reports. Match each to test logs, CI jobs, result files, or audit events with the same revision, environment, selection, and timestamp.

content.name: p
content: Compare test counts, skips, failure names, exit status, and completion events with the claim. Inspect wrappers and output-capture errors where a command summary differs from detailed results; look for linked CI evidence when the local transcript is incomplete.

content.name: p
content: The agent reports only the selected passing tests and states that the full suite was not run. The execution record supports the stated scope, so there is no

content.name: ref
content: claim–evidence gap

content.name: p
content: Cached results are labeled with their actual age and revision and used only for a claim they support. They do not contradict the reported freshness or scope in

content.name: ref
content: claim–evidence gap

content.name: p
content: A matching CI record supports the claim even though it is absent from the local transcript. That is not contradictory or demonstrably insufficient execution evidence under

content.name: ref
content: claim–evidence gap
; inaccessible logs alone leave the assessment unresolved.

content.name: p
content: Record the episode identifier and date, task type, model and harness versions, exact claim, claim time, and the verification scope asserted. Preserve command and test selection, executed/passed/failed/skipped counts, exit status, result artifacts, timestamps, revision, environment, wrappers, and output-capture errors. Include external evidence and access gaps, number of verification claims reviewed and contradicted, discrepancy type, subsequent decisions, reruns, and investigation time. Distinguish unknown evidence from a demonstrated contradiction.

content.name: p
content: Synthetic incident: a filtered command passes two tests and the agent reports all 240 passed. The command selection and runner count expose 238 unrun tests; a reviewer’s full-suite run then finds six failures. The incorrect report had hidden the remaining verification work and required another run before review could finish.

content.name: p
content: Reported incident:

content.name: a
content: Claude Code issue #22507

includes a transcript excerpt showing a 10.31-second operation failing a one-second performance limit. The PR description instead blamed a different test and called the failure a pre-existing timeout. Comparing the description with the runner output exposed the misreport; the account describes a rerun and further challenges to reconstruct what happened. It supports inaccurate reporting, not the title’s assertion that no tests ran.

content.name: p
content: Synthetic comparison: the agent reports two targeted tests passed and 238 other tests remain unrun. The selection and runner output support the stated scope. The verification is limited, but the reader can see the remaining work without reconstructing a false full-suite claim.

documents.summary: An agent reduces verification’s ability to detect an unmet requirement while working on the problem that verification is meant to expose.
documents.title: Weakening the checks

content.name: summary
content: An agent reduces verification’s ability to detect an unmet requirement while working on the problem that verification is meant to expose.

content.name: p
content: While addressing a requirement or failure, the agent changes verification so that behavior violating that requirement is no longer detected. There is no valid replacement check, authorized requirement change, or approved deferral that explicitly leaves the requirement unresolved.

content.name: p
content: Compare the requirement with before-and-after test code, CI configuration, fixtures, and result artifacts. Look for removed assertions, skips, narrowed selections, relaxed comparisons, replaced dependencies, and success-code handling.

content.name: p
content: Trace a known failing input or other counterexample through the old and new checks to see what detection changed. Compare contract revisions, approvals, and replacement tests for evidence that a changed check still serves the intended requirement.

content.name: p
content: An authorized behavior change invalidates the old assertion and replacement verification covers the new contract. The authorized requirement change excludes this from

content.name: ref
content: reduced detection

content.name: p
content: Redundant tests are consolidated and the replacement still detects the relevant violating behaviors. Detection is preserved rather than reduced under

content.name: ref
content: reduced detection

content.name: p
content: An unavailable integration is deferred with approval and its acceptance criterion remains explicitly unresolved. This is the approved deferral excluded by

content.name: ref
content: reduced detection
, rather than a check silently counted as satisfied.

content.name: p
content: Record the episode identifier and date, task type, model and harness versions, original requirement, and known failing behavior. Preserve before-and-after check code, configuration, test selections and skip counts, reports, contract changes, approvals, and replacement coverage. Include the counterexamples detected before and after, requirements left unresolved, changes presented as successful, escaped defects, rollback or repair time, and final outcome. Retain total checks or requirements assessed to distinguish incident counts from rates.

content.name: p
content: Synthetic incident: a function must return sorted results, but the agent changes its test to sort both expected and actual values before comparison. A diff and replay of three unsorted fixtures show all three changing from fail to pass without a function fix. The ordering defect remains, the check can no longer catch it, and QA reopens the task.

content.name: p
content: Reported incident:

content.name: a
content: Claude Code issue #4882

describes replacing test imports with skips and placeholders despite an explicit requirement for real implementations. The supplied health-check example skips the database-backed check, making the missing verification visible in code review. The reporter describes noncompliant work requiring user intervention; affected-test counts and rework duration are not supplied, and the report does not establish intentional gaming.

content.name: p
content: Synthetic comparison: the user changes an API contract from ordered to unordered output. The updated test accepts three differently ordered results but still rejects missing or extra items. Comparing the approval, contract, and test cases shows preserved checking of the new requirement rather than concealment of an old failure.

documents.summary: An agent reverses a substantive conclusion toward a user’s assertion without establishing evidence or reasoning that supports the reversal.
documents.title: Agreement-driven reversal

content.name: summary
content: An agent reverses a substantive conclusion toward a user’s assertion without establishing evidence or reasoning that supports the reversal.

content.name: p
content: After a user challenges a substantive conclusion, the agent adopts the user’s opposing claim or reverses related work while providing no adequate new evidence, applicable premise, or reasoning to support that change. The earlier and later positions concern the same factual or technical question.

content.name: p
